why: \(\ln\) is only defined for positive numbers, so \(6 - 2x > 0\), giving \(x < 3\). At \(x = 3\) the log would be of 0, which is undefined.

prompt: What is the derivative of \(\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x}{3}\)?
why: \(\frac{d}{dx}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{a} = \frac{a}{a^2 + x^2}\). With \(a = 3\): \(\frac{3}{9 + x^2}\). (By the chain rule: \(\frac{1}{1 + x^2/9} \times \frac{1}{3}\).)

The graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis (even), so the top is \(x^2\). It approaches \(y = 1\) for large \(x\), which needs the same leading coefficients top and bottom, and between \(\pm 2\) it is negative, so the bottom is \(x^2 - 4\). (\(\frac{x^2}{4 - x^2}\) would approach \(y = -1\).)

prompt: A particle starts from rest, 3 metres to the right of the origin, and moves along the \(x\)-axis in simple harmonic motion with a period of 4 seconds. Which equation could represent the motion of the particle?
why: Starting from rest at \(x = 3\) means 3 is an end point: \(x = 3\cos nt\) has \(x = 3\) and \(\dot{x} = 0\) at \(t = 0\). The period is \(\frac{2\pi}{n} = 4\), so \(n = \frac{\pi}{2}\). (\(\cos 4t\) has period \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), not 4.)

prompt: It is given that \(\cos x = -\dfrac{1}{3}\), where \(\dfrac{\pi}{2} < x < \pi\). What is the value of \(\sin 2x\)?
why: In the second quadrant \(\sin x > 0\): \(\sin x = \sqrt{1 - \frac{1}{9}} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\). So \(\sin 2x = 2\sin x\cos x = 2 \times \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} \times \left(-\frac{1}{3}\right) = -\frac{4\sqrt{2}}{9}\). (\(-\frac{7}{9}\) is \(\cos 2x\).)

prompt: Let \(P(x) = qx^3 + rx^2 - rx - q\), where \(q\) and \(r\) are constants and \(q \ne 0\). One of the zeros of \(P(x)\) is 1. Given that \(\alpha\) is a zero of \(P(x)\) and \(\alpha \ne 1\), which of the following is also a zero?
why: The product of the roots is \(-\frac{-q}{q} = 1\). One root is 1, so the other two multiply to 1: the third root is \(\frac{1}{\alpha}\). (Check: \(x^3P\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) = -P(x)\), so \(\frac{1}{\alpha}\) is a root whenever \(\alpha\) is.)

prompt: In how many ways can all the letters of the word COMMITTEE be placed in a line with the two Ts next to each other?
why: Glue the two Ts into one block: that leaves 8 items, C, O, M, M, I, TT, E, E, with M and E each repeated twice: \(\frac{8!}{2!\,2!}\). The Ts inside the block are identical, so there is no extra \(2!\) for swapping them.

prompt: Which graph best represents \(y = \sin^{-1}(\cos x)\), for \(0 \le x \le \pi\)?
why: \(\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)\), and for \(0 \le x \le \pi\), \(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\) lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), the range of \(\sin^{-1}\). So \(y = \frac{\pi}{2} - x\): a straight line from \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) down to \(\left(\pi, -\frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

\(f\) has domain \(x \ge -2\) and range \(y \le -\sqrt{2}\), so \(f^{-1}\) is only the part of the quartic with \(x \le -\sqrt{2}\) (the left-hand arm, rising from \((-\sqrt{2}, -2)\)). Both graphs only exist for \(-2 \le x \le -\sqrt{2}\), and there \(f\) is decreasing and \(f^{-1}\) is decreasing; they meet once, on the line \(y = x\) (at \(x = -\frac{1 + \sqrt{5}}{2}\)). stmt_text: For what values of x is \dfrac{x}{x - 2} < 3?
sol_text:

Multiply both sides by (x - 2)^2 > 0: x(x - 2) < 3(x - 2)^2, x \ne 2.

So (x - 2)(x - 3) > 0: x < 2 or x > 3.

stmt_text: A particle moves along the x-axis in simple harmonic motion, with position x = \sqrt{3}\cos 2t + 3\sin 2t for t \ge 0.(i) Write x in the form R\cos(2t - \alpha), where R > 0 and 0 < \alpha < \dfrac{\pi}{2}. 2(ii) Find the two values of x where the particle comes to rest. 1(iii) When is the first time that the speed of the particle is half of its maximum speed? 2
sol_text:
Model answer:
(i) R\cos\alpha = \sqrt{3} and R\sin\alpha = 3, so R = \sqrt{3 + 9} = 2\sqrt{3} and \tan\alpha = \sqrt{3}, \alpha = \frac{\pi}{3}: x = 2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(2t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right).
(ii) The particle is at rest at the ends of the motion: x = \pm 2\sqrt{3}.
(iii) \dot{x} = -4\sqrt{3}\sin\left(2t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right), maximum speed 4\sqrt{3}. Half of it needs \left|\sin\left(2t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right| = \frac{1}{2}.
At t = 0, 2t - \frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac{\pi}{3} and |\sin| = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, which is too big; it first drops to \frac{1}{2} at 2t - \frac{\pi}{3} = -\frac{\pi}{6}, so t = \frac{\pi}{12} s.

(ii) The particle is at rest at the ends of the motion: \(x = \pm 2\sqrt{3}\).

(iii) \(\dot{x} = -4\sqrt{3}\sin\left(2t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\), maximum speed \(4\sqrt{3}\). Half of it needs \(\left|\sin\left(2t - \frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right| = \frac{1}{2}\).

By the focus-directrix property, SP = PM = 3p^2 - (-3) = 3p^2 + 3.

prompt:
Prove by mathematical induction that, for all integers \(n \ge 1\),
\(\dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{2}{3!} + \dfrac{3}{4!} + \cdots + \dfrac{n}{(n + 1)!} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{(n + 1)!}\).
stmt_text: Prove by mathematical induction that, for all integers n \ge 1,\dfrac{1}{2!} + \dfrac{2}{3!} + \dfrac{3}{4!} + \cdots + \dfrac{n}{(n + 1)!} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{(n + 1)!}.
sol_text:
Model answer:
Step 1. n = 1: LHS = \frac{1}{2}, RHS = 1 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}. True.
Step 2. Assume true for n = k: \displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{k} \frac{r}{(r + 1)!} = 1 - \frac{1}{(k + 1)!}.
Step 3. For n = k + 1: LHS = 1 - \dfrac{1}{(k + 1)!} + \dfrac{k + 1}{(k + 2)!} = 1 - \dfrac{(k + 2) - (k + 1)}{(k + 2)!} = 1 - \dfrac{1}{(k + 2)!}, the RHS for n = k + 1.
So if true for n = k, it is true for n = k + 1; since true for n = 1, by induction it is true for all n \ge 1.

stmt_text: The diagram shows the graph of y = \dfrac{2}{x - k}, where k is a positive real number. [diagram] (i) By considering the graphs of y = x^2 and y = \dfrac{2}{x - k}, explain why the function f(x) = x^3 - kx^2 - 2 has exactly one real zero. 2Let this zero be \alpha, and let x_1 = k be a first approximation to \alpha.(ii) Show that one application of Newton's method gives a second approximation x_2 = k + \dfrac{2}{k^2}. 2(iii) Show that x_1 < \alpha < x_2. 3
sol_text:
Model answer:
(i) f(x) = 0 means x^2(x - k) = 2, that is x^2 = \frac{2}{x - k} (x \ne k). For x < k, \frac{2}{x - k} < 0 \le x^2, so there is no meeting point. For x > k, x^2 increases from k^2 while \frac{2}{x - k} decreases from \infty to 0, so they cross exactly once. So f has exactly one real zero, and it is greater than k.
(ii) f(k) = k^3 - k^3 - 2 = -2 and f'(x) = 3x^2 - 2kx, so f'(k) = k^2. x_2 = k - \dfrac{-2}{k^2} = k + \dfrac{2}{k^2}.
(iii) f(x_1) = -2 < 0.
f(x_2) = x_2^2(x_2 - k) - 2 = \left(k + \frac{2}{k^2}\right)^2 \times \frac{2}{k^2} - 2 = 2\left[\left(1 + \frac{2}{k^3}\right)^2 - 1\right] > 0.
f is continuous, so it has a zero between x_1 and x_2. Since \alpha is the only zero, x_1 < \alpha < x_2.
